text:
Your checkout has a gateman. And he's chasing your students away.

About 7 in 10 online carts never get paid for (Baymard Institute, 50 studies). Surprise fees, a page people don't trust, forced accounts, long forms, errors. They wanted in. The gate stopped them.

How many steps does it take to pay you? Count them tonight and comment the number.

#lagoslogic #checkout #onlinecoach #coursecreator #salesfunnel
alts: Slide 1 of 8. Lagos Logic. Your checkout has a gateman.
Slide 2 of 8. You know him. “Oga, who you come see?” Write your name. Drop your ID. Wait while I call your host. By the third question, visitors start turning back.
Slide 3 of 8. Online, the gate is your checkout. About 7 in 10 online carts never get paid for. That's the average across 50 studies of online checkouts. They wanted it. The gate stopped them.

Slide 4 of 8. The gateman's questions · 1 of 2. Why people walk away. “Why is there a ₦2,500 fee on top?”, 40 percent · extra costs: Show the full price, fees included, on the sales page. “Can I trust this page with my card?”, 19 percent · trust: Use a payment page people know. Offer bank transfer too. Show your name and number. “Create an account? I just want to pay.”, 18 percent · forced account: Let them pay first. Create their login for them after.

Slide 5 of 8. The gateman's questions · 2 of 2. Why people walk away. “Why are there 3 pages of forms?”, 17 percent · long checkout: Before payment, ask for name, email and WhatsApp. Nothing else. “Error. Try again later.”, 17 percent · site errors: Test your own payment link on a cheap phone every week.

Slide 6 of 8. On WhatsApp too. Same gateman. Different uniform. “Send your full name, email, phone number, occupation, state, how you heard about us and your goals for the program.” Before they've even paid. Ask for 3 things now. Collect the rest after payment.
Slide 7 of 8. Count your gates. From “I want in” to paid. 3 steps. Every extra step is a gateman. They see the price. They tap pay. They get the class link.
Slide 8 of 8. Your turn. How many steps does it take to pay you? Count them tonight. Comment the number. Photo of Agoro Hassan.

text:
How to answer “Can you reduce the price?” without cutting it.

A vague price invites bargaining. Make it feel final: write the rule once, show the bigger option first, give 3 choices. Make it feel fair: say what's included, trade instead of cutting, walk away kindly.

Trade. Never cut. Every cut teaches your buyers to ask again.

What do you reply? Comment it and I'll sharpen the first 10.

#pricing #salestips #onlinecoach #coachingbusiness #coursecreator
alts: Slide 1 of 7. Save this. How to answer “Can you reduce the price?” without cutting it.

Slide 2 of 7. Why they ask. A vague price is an invitation to bargain. If your price looks like a starting point, it is one. Market habits come online. Your job is to make the price feel final, and fair.

Slide 3 of 7. Tactics 1 to 3. Make it feel final. Write the rule once: “The price is fixed. Pay in 2 parts is available.” Pin it. Save it as a quick reply. Show the bigger option first. Next to ₦250,000 for 1:1, the ₦75,000 group program feels easy. Give 3 choices, not 1: self paced, group, 1:1. People compare your options, not your price.

Slide 4 of 7. Tactics 4 to 6. Make it feel fair. Say what's included: live classes, replays, templates, WhatsApp support. Trade, never cut: add a bonus call instead of reducing the price. Walk away kindly: “No wahala. The next cohort opens in January if the timing is better.”

Slide 5 of 7. Tactic 5 in action. You kept your price. They still got a win. Message: Can you reduce the price small? Message: The price is fixed at ₦75,000. But if you join by Friday, I'll add a 1:1 call in week 1. Message: Ok. Send the payment link.
Slide 6 of 7. The rule. Trade. Never cut. Give something that costs you little and means a lot to them: a bonus call, early access, a template pack. Every cut teaches your buyers to ask again.
Slide 7 of 7. Your turn. What do you reply to “Can you reduce the price?” Comment your reply. I'll sharpen the first 10. Photo of Agoro Hassan.

text:
“Can you reduce the price?” lands in every coach's inbox.

Cutting the price once teaches buyers to ask every time. Trading works better: keep the price, add something that costs you little and means a lot to them, like a bonus call, early access or a template pack.

Example: “The price is fixed at ₦75,000. But if you join by Friday, I'll add a 1:1 call in week 1.” (price is an example)

How do you answer it?

Your ad isn't bad. The place it sends people is.

The board said CMS. The bus went to Ikorodu. If your ad says “free class” and the page asks for ₦5,000, or the ad shows your face and the page shows stock photos, people get down at the next stop.

Slide 5 of 7. The 10 second match test. Open your ad and your page side by side. Same words? Same offer? Same price? Same face? Four yeses, and the bus goes where the board says.
Slide 6 of 7. Also check. Your DM is a landing page too. If the ad says “Send CLASS to join”, your first reply must match the ad. Same price. Same offer. Same energy.

Your free class WhatsApp group is a classroom. Most of them look abandoned.

No welcome. No rules. Last message: “Is the class still holding?” So people mute it, then leave.

#whatsappmarketing #masterclass #onlinecoach #coursecreator #community
alts: Slide 1 of 8. WhatsApp groups. Your free class WhatsApp group is a classroom. Most of them look abandoned.
Slide 2 of 8. Signs it's abandoned. No welcome. No rules. Last message: “Is the class still holding?” Nobody knows what happens next. So they mute it, then leave.

Slide 3 of 8. Bring it back · 1 to 4. Set it up once. A welcome message: what this group is for, and when class happens. 3 rules: no spam, no selling, questions welcome. A pinned message: the date, the time, the link. Admins only for the first hour, so everyone sees the welcome.

Slide 4 of 8. Bring it back · 5 to 7. Then keep it alive. One useful post a day before class: a tip, a question, a student win. Reminders: the day before, the morning of, 1 hour before. A clear end: the offer, the deadline, then close the group.

Slide 5 of 8. Example welcome message. Message: Welcome! This group is for Saturday's free class: how to land your first 3 coaching clients. Class: Sat 10am on Zoom. The link comes here Saturday morning. Introduce yourself: name, city, and what you coach.

Slide 6 of 8. Example post · 2 days before. People show up for what they've already started. Message: Quick homework before Saturday: write down the last 3 questions people asked you about your work. Bring them. We'll turn them into your first offer.

Slide 7 of 8. After the class. Close the group on purpose. Post the offer and the deadline. Answer questions for 48 hours. Then close it, and move everyone who wants more to your broadcast list. A group that dies slowly teaches people to ignore you.

Slide 2 of 8. One review. Quote from Trustpilot reviewer, Aug 2026: I spent over £14,000 with [the company] and, in my experience, received nothing of meaningful value in return, not even genuine opportunities to quote for work, let alone a realistic chance of winning projects.
Slide 3 of 8. Another. Quote from Trustpilot reviewer, Sept 2026: Over £1,000 spent. Seven months. Zero leads. AVOID.

Slide 4 of 8. The line that says it all. Quote from Trustpilot reviewer, Aug 2026: I wasn't paying [the company] to generate salespeople wanting to sell to me. I was paying them to generate customers wanting to buy from me.
Slide 5 of 8. What went wrong. They paid for activity. They wanted customers. Clicks, reports, and “leads” that were really other sellers. Nobody agreed in writing what a result was.

Slide 6 of 8. Their own advice. Quote from Trustpilot reviewer, Aug 2026: Ask exactly how much of your monthly payment will actually be spent with Google/Meta. Ask exactly what [the company] keeps. Get the definition of a "lead" in writing.

Slide 7 of 8. Before you sign anything. 4 questions. What part of my money reaches Google or Meta? What counts as a lead or a result, in writing? What happens if the results don't come? Can I leave without a penalty?
Slide 8 of 8. Protect your money. Save this before your next contract. My rule: you keep every login, and we agree in writing what done means before you pay. Photo of Agoro Hassan.
